processing: A cultivar bred for sencha, normally steamed, rolled and dried in the usual way. It has also been tested as steamed tamaryokucha and appears in some matcha.
harvest_season: A late cultivar, budding about 3 to 5 days after Yabukita; the spring flush is the prized one, as usual for sencha.
appearance_dry: As sencha, typically deep green, fine needles.
appearance_liquor: Typically a clear yellow-green, as with other steamed sencha.
appearance_wet: Soft green leaf, typical of a steamed sencha.
taste_profile: Strong umami with little bitterness or astringency, and a mellow, sweet aroma that is clearly different from Yabukita's.

brewing.notes: Cooler water suits its low-astringency, savoury character. The second steep is short, as usual for sencha.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring sencha, usually as a single-cultivar lot from a small producer or blended away without being named. As with other sencha it is best within about a year of picking. Being a late budder, it reaches the market a little after the early cultivars.
description:
Harumidori is a modern Japanese cultivar with a very clear aim: a late-budding, high-yielding sencha tea that does not just taste like Yabukita. Its registered number is Cha Norin 48.

Its chemistry makes the case. It is low in tannins and high in amino acids, which reads in the cup as savoury and soft. Processing is the normal sencha route, so the character you taste comes from the plant and not from anything clever in the factory.

Expect strong umami, little bitterness and a mellow sweet aroma. Single-cultivar sencha like this is forgiving of cooler water and shows less at boiling, where you would only pull more astringency out of the leaf.

The name is rarely on a label unless a shop is selling it for its cultivar. Prefectural trials have also looked at it for steamed tamaryokucha, and it has appeared in organic matcha, so it is not limited to needle sencha.

A good next step is tasting it against a plain Yabukita sencha from the same year. The aromas are different enough that even a beginner tends to notice.
history:
Harumidori was bred at the Makurazaki station of Japan's national vegetable and tea research organisation in Kagoshima. It comes from a 1972 cross with Kanayamidori as seed parent and Yabukita as pollen parent, and was registered in 2000 as Cha Norin 48.

Prefectural research stations went on to trial it. Shizuoka reported relatively good cold tolerance and yields at or above Yabukita, with slow early growth after planting and weakness to anthracnose among the drawbacks.
sources_note: name_zh is a plain rendering of the kana name, not an established Chinese name.
